claims.text: Annealing HfZrTiTa0.53 at approximately 650°C for 30 minutes followed by controlled slow cooling will produce fine-scale intragranular precipitates.
The annealing-induced precipitates will relieve internal stress concentrations.
The annealing-induced precipitates will enhance dislocation mobility.
The treatment will increase tensile uniform elongation by 30–50%, from approximately 13.5% to roughly 17–20%.
The treatment will preserve yield strength above approximately 750 MPa.
The treatment will preserve compressive strength near 1300 MPa.
The treatment will preserve the alloy's impact-triggered chemical energy release.
As-cast HfZrTiTa0.53 has approximately 13.5% tensile uniform elongation.
As-cast HfZrTiTa0.53 has a yield strength of approximately 786 MPa and a compressive strength of approximately 1314 MPa.
HfZrTiTa0.53 has established energetic-release properties in penetration tests.
A parametric annealing study from 600°C to 700°C for 30 minutes with varied controlled cooling rates will be used to optimize precipitate size and distribution.
Fine intragranular precipitates will selectively relax grain-boundary stress concentrations without significantly coarsening the primary matrix.
Controlled precipitation at sub-critical annealing temperatures will activate additional slip systems during tensile loading.
Excessive precipitate coarsening will cause a significant reduction in strength.
The ductility prediction applies to room-temperature uniaxial tensile loading at a strain rate around 10^-4 s^-1.
Energetic performance will be assessed using high-strain-rate impact tests above 500 s^-1.
Annealing significantly above 650°C or cooling too rapidly may cause precipitate coarsening and degradation of mechanical properties.

Failure to achieve at least a 30% statistically significant increase in tensile uniform elongation while retaining at least approximately 750 MPa yield strength and impact energy release will falsify the hypothesis.
